subject: technology
topic: A notification breaks your focus even if you never look
angle: While notifications cause measurable performance drops and strain, their impact varies depending on task difficulty, the timing of the interruption, and the mere presence of a device.
title: The Weight of Presence

hooks.text: Does your phone affect you when it is silent?
You think you are focused, but the device is distracting you.
You carry a weight that slows your thoughts.
A dark screen sits on a wooden table.
Presence is enough to disrupt your mind.

reveal.headline: The mere presence of a smartphone lowers your performance.
reveal.body: You do not have to touch it or look at it. Just having the device within reach reduces your cognitive ability.

explain.headline: Your task difficulty determines the impact.
explain.body: Notifications disrupt fast, stimulus-driven searches more than slow, effortful tasks. However, when a task is difficult, forced multitasking leads to significantly lower performance.

matters.headline: The timing of a notification matters.
matters.body: Interruptions early in a search task are linked to forgetting the primary goal. That may be why your focus feels fractured the moment you start something new.

example.headline: A phone sits on the desk next to your laptop.
example.body: You are trying to write a report. The screen stays dark. You still feel your concentration thinning as you glance toward it.

question.headline: Where does your focus go when you aren't looking?

stat.label: the result of the mere presence of a smartphone

claims.text: The mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance.
claims.quote: The results of the conducted experiment imply that the mere presence of a smartphone results in lower cognitive performance, which supports the hypothesis of the smartphone presence using limited cognitive resources.

claims.text: Interruptions coming early during a search task are more likely to result in the user forgetting the primary task goal than interruptions that arrive later on.
claims.quote: In addition, we show that interruptions coming early during a search task are more likely to result in the user forgetting the primary task goal than interruptions that arrive later on.

claims.text: There is a general tendency to resume tasks, but no memory advantage for unfinished tasks.
claims.quote: We found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks but found a general tendency to resume tasks.

claims.text: Notifications are more disruptive for fast, stimulus-driven search tasks than for slower, more effortful semantic-based search tasks.
claims.quote: Our findings replicate earlier work, showing the generally harmful effects of IM, and further show that notifications are more disruptive for fast, stimulus-driven search tasks than for slower, more effortful semantic-based search tasks.

claims.text: When the primary task was considered difficult, subjects forced to multitask had significantly lower performance compared with not only the subjects who did not multitask but also the subjects who were able to multitask at their discretion.
claims.quote: The results show that when the primary task was considered difficult, subjects forced to multitask had significantly lower performance compared with not only the subjects who did not multitask but also the subjects who were able to multitask at their discretion.

claims.text: Reducing notification-caused interruptions is beneficial for performance and reducing strain.
claims.quote: The findings revealed that a reduction of notification-caused interruptions is beneficial for performance and reducing strain.

verdict: The evidence confirms that notifications and the presence of smartphones disrupt cognitive performance and memory, though the severity depends on the specific nature of the task being performed.
caveat: The research does not fully explain the specific role of anxiety in impeding performance when notifications are disabled.
caption:
Your focus is being shaped by things you do not see.

Research shows that the mere presence of a smartphone lowers cognitive performance. The impact varies based on task difficulty and timing, though the role of anxiety is not yet fully explained.

How often do you feel your concentration slip when your phone is nearby?
